lesson.title: Who Does This Apply To: Scope of Inference
lesson.summary: Covers how the way individuals were selected and, in an experiment, how they were assigned to treatments together determine what conclusions, causal or merely associative, can be generalized to which group.
lesson.body:
Two separate questions get conflated constantly when people talk about a study's results: to whom can this result be generalized, and can this result be described as caused by the treatment. Neither question is answered by looking at the results themselves, the p-value or the size of the difference. Both are answered by design choices made before a single data point was collected, specifically how the individuals in the study were chosen, and, if it was an experiment, how they were assigned to groups.

It helps to lay out all four combinations. Random selection from a population combined with random assignment to treatments, a randomized experiment run on a randomly chosen sample, supports a causal conclusion that generalizes to the full population. Random selection without random assignment, a well-designed observational study or sample survey, supports generalizing to the population, but only in terms of association, never causation. Random assignment without random selection, the common case of a classroom or volunteer experiment, supports a causal claim, but only for the specific group that was studied, extending it to a wider population is a judgment call about how similar that group is to the wider world, not something the statistics itself guarantees. And a study with neither kind of randomization supports neither confident generalization nor a causal claim.

Consider a psychology class that recruits volunteer classmates and randomly assigns half to drink coffee and half to drink a placebo before a reaction time test. Because assignment was random, a real difference in average reaction time between the groups can be attributed to caffeine, that is a legitimate causal claim, but only about those volunteers. Extending it to all adults requires an extra, non-statistical argument that the volunteers resemble adults generally in the ways that matter, an argument the randomization itself does nothing to support, since the volunteers were never randomly selected from a larger population in the first place.

This connects directly to the study limitations you just worked through. Undercoverage or non-response at the sampling stage narrows what a study can generalize to even when every later calculation is done flawlessly, because no amount of correct arithmetic can speak for the people who were never given a chance to be included. Spotting a generalizability problem uses the exact same close reading of the study's design that spotting a limitation does, they are really the same skill pointed at two related questions.

On a free-response question, whenever you are asked whether results can be generalized to some group, or whether a causal statement is justified, answer by pointing at the actual design, how subjects were selected and how treatments were assigned, rather than at the sample size or how strong the observed effect looks. A huge, striking effect from a poorly designed study still cannot be generalized or called causal beyond what the design supports. Generalizability is a design question, not a computational one.
